identification.summary: SHARK SPIDER is a criminal (eCrime) actor name associated with the Shylock banking Trojan, also called Caphaw by some vendors; the actor's activity is described as first observed in November 2013 and aimed at online banking and Bitcoin wallet credentials. The Shylock malware itself dates to 2011 and uses man-in-the-browser attacks against customers of a preset list of banks [S7][S9]. Microsoft detects the threat as Win32/Caphaw [S2]. The actor name and November 2013 date come from the Malpedia entry (the existing record's source) that this research could not open or date [S9].
identification.firstObserved: 2013-11 (actor activity, per Malpedia text); malware first discovered 2011
identification.notes: Shylock/Caphaw is a malware family; this research found no source tying the SHARK SPIDER label to a named vendor report, and could not confirm CrowdStrike authorship of the name. Microsoft has no name in the existing record.

attribution.sponsor: Unattributed financially motivated criminal group; no state sponsor found in sources
attribution.confidence: Low (origin only). Symantec, as reported by Tech Monitor, considered the controlling gang likely based in Russia or eastern Europe [S6].
attribution.basis: Vendor assessment of likely geography only (Symantec via Tech Monitor) [S6]. The 2014 law enforcement action reported no arrests [S5][S7], so no individual attribution is public in the sources reviewed.

objectives: Financial theft: access funds in business or personal bank accounts and transfer them to the criminal operators [S2]; the actor description also cites theft of Bitcoin wallet credentials [S9].

sectors: Banking and financial services customers (business and personal accounts)
targeting.notes: Europol and the NCA said the UK was the main target, with the US, Italy and Turkey also targeted [S2]. ESET reported Caphaw attacking major European banks via a webinject plugin in February 2013 [S4]. At least 30,000 Windows machines were reported infected worldwide [S1][S2]; Dark Reading reported over 60,000 infections detected in the prior year [S8].

capabilities.summary: Man-in-the-browser banking Trojan that injects web content into browsers and steals banking credentials [S7]. Modular plugin architecture covering command-and-control communication, configuration file, plugins and anti-analysis techniques [S5]. Self-propagation: a Skype plugin (msg.gsm per CSIS Denmark) uses Skype chat to send links to a victim's contacts [S3]; Symantec module names include DiskSpread (removable drives) and MsgSpread (Skype) [S7]. Infection typically began with victims clicking malicious links and running the downloaded malware [S2]. The Trojan runs in memory, deletes its installation files and reinstalls after reboot [S7]. Infrastructure used proxy servers and redundant C&C [S7]. No exploited CVEs are tied to the actor in sources reviewed.

campaigns.name: Shylock first discovered
campaigns.summary: Shylock banking Trojan first discovered, using man-in-the-browser attacks against banking customers [S7][S9].

campaigns.name: Skype-spreading variant
campaigns.summary: A new Shylock version reported spreading through Skype; CSIS Denmark identified a plugin named msg.gsm that messages the victim's contacts with links [S3].

campaigns.name: Caphaw webinject against European banks
campaigns.summary: ESET reported Caphaw attacking major European banks using a webinject plugin [S4].

campaigns.name: Share of banking malware
campaigns.summary: Dell SecureWorks put Shylock at 7% of all banking malware in 2013 [S7].

campaigns.name: NCA-led international takedown
campaigns.summary: On 8-9 July 2014 the UK NCA, with EC3, the FBI and counterparts in Italy, the Netherlands, Turkey, Germany, France and Poland, plus BAE Systems Applied Intelligence, Dell SecureWorks, Kaspersky Lab and GCHQ, seized C&C servers and domains; announced 10 July. At least 30,000 Windows machines were infected; Microsoft added Win32/Caphaw detection to MSRT; no arrests reported [S1][S2][S5][S7].

diamond.adversary: Unidentified criminal group; likely Russia or eastern Europe per Symantec [S6]. Source code was never leaked or sold in sources reviewed, suggesting a single group wrote and ran it (search-summary inference; verify) [S5].
diamond.capability: Modular banking Trojan with man-in-the-browser injection, Skype and removable-drive spreading, in-memory persistence [S3][S5][S7].
diamond.infrastructure: Command-and-control servers and communication domains, with proxy servers and redundant C&C; seized July 2014 [S2][S7].
diamond.victim: Online banking customers, principally in the UK, with US, Italy, Turkey and Europe also affected [S2][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Profit-driven cybercrime; no state tasking found in sources [S6].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints, web browsers, Skype, removable media, online banking sessions [S3][S7].

gaps: Could not confirm a vendor report that defines SHARK SPIDER; the label and the November 2013 date rest on the Malpedia text, which could not be opened or dated [S9].
WebFetch was unavailable (network errors); all facts are from search result summaries, not full documents.
Primary documents not opened: NCA and Europol press releases, Dell SecureWorks, Kaspersky/Securelist overview, Symantec and Trusteer reports.
No individual attribution, arrests or post-2014 activity found; whether the actor resumed operations is unknown.
Bitcoin wallet targeting is cited only from the actor description, not a technical report.
Overlap between the SHARK SPIDER actor label and Shylock/Caphaw malware naming across vendors is not reconciled.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Step 1-2: the threat is a criminal banking-malware operation affecting Windows endpoints and online banking, with a UK, US, Italy and Turkey focus [S2]; relevance to military networks is mainly via personal or contractor banking use and shared Skype or removable media on unmanaged hosts [S3][S7]. Step 3-4: MLCOA is opportunistic credential theft through link lures and Skype chat spreading [S2][S3]; MDCOA would be reuse of the modular plugin model against other targets, which sources do not show. Candidate indicators: Skype messages with links from contacts, msg.gsm-style plugin activity, removable-drive spreading, and detection names Win32/Caphaw or Shylock [S2][S3][S7]. Activity appears dormant since the 2014 takedown [S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: treat as historical commodity eCrime with no sourced current activity [S5]. Authorities: response is law enforcement and industry led (NCA, EC3, FBI), not military [S2]. Mission assurance: restrict consumer messaging (Skype) and removable media on mission systems and keep endpoint detection for Caphaw/Shylock families current [S3][S7]. Coordination: route any residual indicators to cyber defense and law enforcement partners through established channels [S2].

provenance.importedSummary: This group's activity was first observed in November 2013. It leverages a banking Trojan more commonly known as Shylock which aims to compromise online banking credentials and credentials related to Bitcoin wallets.
